sources.rank_basis: tier B: Robert C. Martin's personal blog (page header 'by Robert C. Martin (Uncle Bob)'). Rank 1 could also fit because Martin originated ISP, but this is a 2020 retrospective post on a personal blog, not the concept's original publication; two ranks fit, so the higher number (6, personal blog) applies.

tier B: Martin Fowler's personal bliki. Not the originator: the page itself credits the notion to Trygve Reenskaug and Robert Martin ('this notion has been around for a long time'). Not a company or project engineering blog, so personal blog, Rank 6.
tier B: Martin Fowler's personal bliki, a five-sentence entry that defers to RoleInterface for details; personal blog, Rank 6.

claim_checks.claim: A broad interface forces consumers to depend on methods they do not use, and Martin notes that such compile-time dependencies can force recompilation or redeployment even without runtime use.
claim_checks.page_says: when module A depends on module B at compile time, but not at run time, then changes to module B will force recompilation and redeployment of module A.
claim_checks.note: The first clause matches the page's statement of ISP (keep interfaces small so users do not end up depending on things they do not need). The second clause is weaker than the page ('can' for 'will'). Grounding passes; the citation itself breaches rank quarantine (see violations).

claim_checks.claim: Header interfaces that copy every public method of a class hide the actual collaboration, while role interfaces show the methods a specific consumer needs.
claim_checks.page_says: The strength of a role interface is that it clearly communicates the actual collaboration between an activity and its successors.
claim_checks.note: The page says role interfaces communicate the collaboration and show which methods are needed; it never says header interfaces 'hide' it. 'Hide' is a stronger statement than the contrast the page draws.

claim_checks.claim: A role interface is shaped by one supplier-consumer interaction; the same supplier may implement several such roles.
claim_checks.page_says: A role interface is defined by looking at a specific interaction between suppliers and consumers. A supplier component will usually implement several role interfaces
claim_checks.note: 'May implement several' is weaker than the page's 'will usually implement several'. Grounding passes; the citation breaches rank quarantine.

claim_checks.claim: A header interface mirrors a class's full public surface and tends to force implementers to provide methods irrelevant to their role.
claim_checks.page_says: Essentially you take all the public methods of a class and declare them in an interface.
claim_checks.note: The first half is entailed. The second half (forcing implementers to provide unneeded methods) is not on the cited HeaderInterface page, which only defers to RoleInterface for pros and cons. The statement is on the uncited RoleInterface page [^2] ('forces you to implement every method'), which does not count, and [^2] is Rank 6 anyway.

claim_checks.claim: TypeScript compatibility is structural, so an object with the required members can satisfy a narrow interface without explicitly naming it.
claim_checks.page_says: Type compatibility in TypeScript is based on structural subtyping. Structural typing is a way of relating types based solely on their members.
claim_checks.note: The Dog/Pet example shows assignment without the class declaring itself an implementer; 'can' leaves room for the object-literal excess-property error the page also shows.

claim_checks.claim: Go idiom favors small method sets such as one-method `Reader` and `Writer` interfaces, named for the operation they provide.
claim_checks.page_says: Interfaces with only one or two methods are common in Go code, and are usually given a name derived from the method, such as io.Writer
claim_checks.note: The page reports that small interfaces are common and gives the -er naming convention for one-method interfaces (Reader, Writer); it does not say Go idiom favors or prefers small method sets. Frequency is written as a preference.

claim_checks.claim: ISP is about consumers being forced beyond their needs.
claim_checks.page_says: Keep interfaces small so that users don’t end up depending on things they don’t need.
claim_checks.note: Row context: 'One consumer needs all methods | A broader interface may be fine'. The page also says splitting is 'often not feasible, nor even desirable', consistent with the row. Rank 6 is allowed in role 6.

claim_checks.claim: Compatibility checks target members, not supplier identity.
claim_checks.page_says: Only members of the target type (Pet in this case) are considered when checking for compatibility.
claim_checks.note: Row context: 'TypeScript extra members | Usually accepted when assigned structurally'. 'Usually' matches the page's exception for object literals with unknown properties.

claim_checks.claim: The role is discovered by use, not by the concrete type's package.
claim_checks.page_says: not found (searched cache/5d82dc9a454d.txt for: consumer, package that uses, near the, placement, discover, small interface)
claim_checks.note: Row context: 'Go interface placement | Define small interfaces near the consumer when practical'. Effective Go says nothing about where to define interfaces; its implicit-satisfaction passage is about how a type implements an interface, not placement. Its Generality section shows the opposite pattern for one case: the implementing side exports the interface (crc32.NewIEEE and adler32.New return hash.Hash32).

claim_checks.claim: The consumer contract can still validate only the fields it needs.
claim_checks.page_says: any type checking involved should only check that the earliest finish data is present. If extra data can be ignored, then it's no crime to supply it
claim_checks.note: Row context: 'Remote API response | Extra fields can travel over the wire'. The claim's 'can' is weaker than the page's 'should only check'.

conflicts.topic: Where a Go interface lives: the doc's Edge cases row says define it near the consumer, while Effective Go's Generality section shows the implementing package exporting the interface (hash.Hash32). Different cases, not a direct contradiction of a roles 1-5 fact; the doc's row sits in role 6 but neither names the Effective Go pattern nor has a source for its own advice.
conflicts.loser: doc's own placement advice, attributed to [^5] without support

violations.evidence: ✅[^1] cites a Rank 6 source (Robert C. Martin's personal blog) in a role 1 section, which allows ranks 1-5.
✅[^2] cites a Rank 6 source (Martin Fowler's bliki) in a role 1 section, which allows ranks 1-5.
✅[^2] (role interface definition) cites a Rank 6 source in a role 3 section, which allows ranks 1-4. The core concept rests on Rank 6 alone.
✅[^3] (header interface definition) cites a Rank 6 source in a role 3 section, which allows ranks 1-4. The core concept rests on Rank 6 alone.
C4 unsupported: 'tends to force implementers to provide methods irrelevant to their role' is not on the cited HeaderInterface page [^3]; only the uncited RoleInterface page says it.
C2 overstates: the page says role interfaces 'clearly communicate the actual collaboration'; the doc says header interfaces 'hide' it, which the page does not say.
C6 overstates: Effective Go says one- or two-method interfaces 'are common in Go code'; the doc says Go idiom 'favors' small method sets.
C9 unsupported: Effective Go [^5] says nothing about defining interfaces near the consumer or roles being discovered by use.

No role 5 (reference and invariants) section: the exact rules the doc relies on (TypeScript's 'at least the same members' rule and its object-literal exception, Go's -er naming convention) are not collected anywhere. Role 2 content (role interface, header interface, supplier, consumer and how they relate) is folded into How it works instead of standing alone without mechanism.
Shows code shapes before and after, but no run: no test double, no call, no compiler result. 'A mock for QuotePage now supplies one operation' is asserted, not shown.

'Class-modeled code uses consumer-owned interfaces for collaborators. Functional-pipeline code uses narrow function types or records of functions at the point of consumption.' is a prescription stated as fact in role 3, with no ✅/⚠️ mark and no citation.
